new_statements.rule_in_words: Stress falls on the final syllable of the word; that syllable is where all the segmental, laryngeal and tonal contrasts are expressed (nasal and laryngealized vowels, central vowels, pre-glottalized/pre-nasalized onsets, phonemic tone, phonetic vowel lengthening all restricted to the final syllable). Corroborated by the JIPA Illustration (Elliott, Edmondson & Sandoval Cruz 2016: 353), which transcribes the Spanish loan lápiz as [la3ˈpi3h] and states that 'stress is shifted from the penultimate to the ultimate syllable', and by Matsukawa 2009 fn. 3 ('a plain vowel is phonetically lengthened in a final syllable').
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned in any opened source.
new_statements.exceptions: None stated for stress. Spanish loanwords are adapted to final stress (JIPA 2016: 353: lápiz > [la3ˈpi3h]; polysyllabic loans lengthen the final vowel). Phonemic tone is otherwise final-syllable only, but future/past aspect forms carry contrastive tone on a non-final syllable (LD&C 2012: 216; JIPA 2016: 360).
new_statements.domain_note: Word level (phonological word including fused enclitics; Matsukawa's statement is made within the phonotactics of the word and generalised to 'Triqui languages'). The statement is a one-clause aside, not a dedicated stress section; the dissertation has no prosody/stress chapter (TOC checked). No instrumental study of stress in this variety was found.
new_statements.identity_note: Matsukawa 2012 describes Chicahuaxtla Triqui (chic1273) from speakers of La Laguna Guadalupe and San Andrés Chicahuaxtla (diss. pp. 21-24); the JIPA Illustration (Elliott, Edmondson & Sandoval Cruz 2016) is based on a San Andrés Chicahuaxtla speaker. Both are the same language-level entry; no dialect split needed. Sister languages Copala Triqui (copa1237) and Itunyoso Triqui (itun1250) are already in the catalog with final prominence.

new_statements.quote:
In polysyllabic words, the penultimate syllable or tonic vowel from Spanish is usually tone 3 (T3), i.e. the default tone in Triqui, while the final syllable, always a vowel unless morphophonologically inflected, lengthens and frequently evidences a lowered tone. [...] The word [la3ˈpi3h] ‘pencil’, from Spanish lápiz [ˈla.pis], retains the original

from Spanish; however, stress is shifted from the penultimate to the ultimate syllable with the addition of a fricative segment [h] to word-final position.

new_statements.relation_note: NOT in the works list for this item (already held by the project from our earlier reading); included because it adds a quotable stress datum. Compatible with the catalog's fixed: final syllable rule: loanword stress is shifted to the ultimate syllable and the final syllable carries length and the contrastive tones. Adds the loanword-adaptation detail; it does not state a native-word stress rule.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No general stress rule is stated, but the only explicit stress remark shows Spanish penultimate stress being moved to the word-final syllable on borrowing ([la3ˈpi3h]), and the final syllable is the locus of vowel lengthening and the full tone contrasts; consistent with final-syllable prominence.
new_statements.exceptions: none; the remark concerns Spanish loanwords, which take final stress even when the source word is penultimate-stressed
new_statements.identity_note: All quoted statements are about Chicahuaxtla Triqui (San Andrés Chicahuaxtla). Matsukawa 2012 p. 143 cites Hollenbach 1984 for loanword stress/tone in Copala Triqui (copa1237), a different Triqui language; not used for this item. Hollenbach 1977 (not opened) compares two Trique dialects, presumably Copala and Chicahuaxtla, so any future reading of it must separate the two.

new_statements.quote: The reason why they do not occur in non-final syllables is unidentified. However, maximum contrasts are expressed in the final syllable, which is stressed, and many sounds do not occur in non-final syllables in Triqui languages. [p. 130] ... The reason why the final syllable rather than the initial syllable attracted tones is probably due to the tendency of tone languages that contour tones occur on the final syllable much more often than on a non-final syllable or that a prominent stressed syllable attracted tones. [p. 364]

new_statements.rule_in_words: The final syllable of the word is the stressed syllable; it is the only syllable carrying the full vowel, length and tone contrasts (non-final syllables have reduced inventories and no phonemic tone). No dedicated stress section; the statement is made in passing in the phonotactics discussion and echoed in the diachronic chapter.
new_statements.exceptions: none stated for Chicahuaxtla. p. 143 (PDF p. 160) cites Hollenbach 1984:147 for COPALA Triqui: tone 4 falls on a long vowel when the Spanish source word has final stress (ko3too4 'cotón') and on a short vowel when the source has penultimate stress (la3pe4 'lápiz') -- that is about Copala, not Chicahuaxtla.
